entries.title: Attempt on Joint scaling limit of all intermediate level sets of the 2D DGFF
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Reduce to tightness plus a characterisation of subsequential limits through the Gibbs-Markov property, uniformly in lambda; try to replace the moment method of Theorem 2.7 by a single martingale approximation of the exponential of a Gaussian field. Result: Partial reduction only. For any finite set of lambdas the vector of point measures is tight (each coordinate is), and any subsequential limit satisfies the Gibbs-Markov property coordinatewise; the coupling question is therefore whether the joint limit is the image of one CGFF under the map lambda -> e^{alpha lambda h} dx with the Seneta-Heyde normalisation. A direct route is to prove the joint limit of the truncated exponentials of the circle-average field at scale epsilon N, whose lambda-dependence is explicit, and then let epsilon -> 0; the missing input is an estimate for the joint contribution of the truncated region uniform in lambda near 1, where the second moment of the measure diverges. Key identity: Z^D_lambda(dx) = lim_eps eps^{lambda^2 alpha^2 g/2} e^{alpha lambda h_eps(x)} dx would identify all Z^D_lambda through one field h. Obstruction: Second moments of Z^D_lambda blow up as lambda -> 1/sqrt2 in the moment method; the uniform-in-lambda control needed for a joint limit up to lambda -> 1 is not available from moment calculations.

entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. entries.title: Attempt on Bypassing the Laplace-transform tail condition for the DGFF extremal measure
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Try to derive the tail exponent from the Gibbs-Markov fixed-point equation as for smoothing transforms (Durrett-Liggett classification). Result: The Gibbs-Markov property along dyadic square partitions gives a fixed-point equation of smoothing type Z^D =_d sum_i e^{alpha Phi_i} Z^{D_i} with Gaussian binding field Phi and 4 pieces; Durrett-Liggett gives, for such equations, that non-trivial solutions have tails whose exponent is the root of a structure equation, here forcing E[Z^D(A)^s] finite iff s < 1. Obstruction: Smoothing-transform theory fixes the power in the tail but not the logarithmic correction; the log factor is what (5) asserts.

entries.title: Attempt on Explicit density of the position of the DGFF maximum
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Express rho^D through the extremal measure and look for a conformal-covariance functional equation that pins it. Result: rho^D(dx) = E[Z^D(dx)/Z^D(D)] where Z^D is the (random) extremal measure; conformal covariance of Z^D gives rho^{f(D)}(f(x)) |f'(x)|^2 = E[ r_D(x)^2 |f'(x)|^{2} ... ] only for the intensity E Z^D(dx) = c r_D(x)^2 dx, not for the ratio, because the normalisation Z^D(D) is not covariant. On the unit disk, rotation invariance gives rho^D radial; a PDE characterisation would need the joint law of (Z^D(dx), Z^D(D)), which is the object Problem 16.1 asks for. Obstruction: rho^D is a ratio expectation; without the law of the total mass Z^D(D) no closed form or PDE is available.

entries.title: Attempt on Existence of the limit of e^{-alpha h} E nu(f_h) for the DGFF cluster law
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Renewal-type argument on the cluster process viewed from the local maximum: depth-h count as a branching-like functional of the concentric decomposition. Result: Writing the cluster as the field pinned at a local maximum, e^{-alpha h} E nu(f_h) is the expected number of points at depth h weighted by e^{-alpha h}; the concentric decomposition expresses the cluster as a random walk with a Bessel-like entropic repulsion plus independent fine fields, so f_h is a sum over scales k <= log(h) of contributions, each of order e^{alpha h} times the probability that the walk is at height h at scale k. A renewal theorem for the walk under entropic repulsion would give the limit; the walk is not a true random walk (steps depend on scale through the binding fields), which is where the existing tools stop. Existence of the limit is therefore reduced to a scale-inhomogeneous renewal theorem. Obstruction: Scale inhomogeneity of the concentric-decomposition walk defeats the standard renewal theorem.

entries.title: Attempt on Universality of level sets and extremal process for log-correlated Gaussian fields in d=2
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Check which steps of the DGFF proof use only the covariance asymptotics and which use the Gibbs-Markov property of the DGFF specifically. Result: The intermediate-level-set moment calculations (Theorem 2.7) use only the two-point Gaussian densities, which are determined by the covariance asymptotics, plus a coarse Gibbs-Markov decoupling at one scale used to identify the limit as unique; for a general field the decoupling can be replaced by the comparison of the field with the DGFF plus an independent bounded-variance field via Kahane-type interpolation, provided the covariance difference is bounded uniformly. Under the hypothesis (16.12) with an additional uniform bound sup |C_N(x,y) - G_N(x,y)| < infinity this gives the Theorem 2.7 analogue by a Gaussian comparison of the exponential moments. The extremal-process part is harder: the cluster law at the maximum depends on the local covariance limit (16.12) and is model-dependent, so universality can only be of the form: same Poisson structure, model-dependent cluster law and constant, which is what the DRZ maximum result already indicates. Obstruction: Without uniform boundedness of C_N - G_N the interpolation fails; with it, the level-set statement follows but the cluster law remains model-dependent.

entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Homogenisation of the Green function at all scales plus the DGFF argument. entries.title: Attempt on Subdiffusive upper bound for the Liouville random walk on the DGFF
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Exit-time lower bound from effective resistance: compare the exit time from B(N) with the commute time. Result: The commute-time identity gives E^0_h tau_{B(N)^c} >= c R_eff(0, B(N)^c) pi(B(N)) where pi is the reversible measure (volume of the Liouville measure of the box). The volume is N^{psi... } of order N^{2 + 2 beta^2 g ...} in the notation of the notes, i.e. N^{psi(beta)} up to N^{o(1)} by the LQG volume estimates, and R_eff(0, B(N)^c) >= (log N)^{1/2 - o(1)} ... the resistance lower bound available is only polylogarithmic. Hence E tau >= N^{psi(beta)} times a polylog, which is the right exponent, but the problem asks for a bound on tau in probability, not in expectation, with a (log T)^{1/2+delta} correction. Converting expectation to probability needs concentration of the exit time, and the exit time is not concentrated at fixed environment because the walk can be trapped near the maximum: the trapping time at the deepest well has a heavy tail. The exponent statement (T^{1/psi(beta)+o(1)}) follows from the expectation bound plus Markov's inequality in one direction; the precise correction is out of reach with the resistance route. Key identity: E tau_B(N) >= c R_eff(0,B(N)^c) mu_h(B(N)) with mu_h(B(N)) = N^{psi(beta)+o(1)}. Obstruction: Exit-time concentration fails at fixed environment because of trapping at deep wells; the polylog correction is a trapping statement, not a resistance statement.

entries.title: Attempt on Limit of the normalised log-effective resistance of the DGFF electric network
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Bound log R_eff by the field along an annulus decomposition; compare upper and lower bounds. Result: Rayleigh monotonicity gives R_eff(x, D_N^c) <= sum over dyadic annuli around x of the resistance across the annulus, each bounded by the maximum of e^{beta h} over the annulus times a constant, so log R_eff <= beta max_{annuli} (h max over annulus) summed... more precisely log R_eff <= log sum_k e^{beta M_k} where M_k is the field maximum over annulus k; by the concentric decomposition M_k is the walk value at scale k plus a bounded extremal term, so log R_eff is bounded above by beta times the maximum over k of the concentric walk, which after dividing by (log N)^{1/2} converges to beta sqrt g times the maximum of a Brownian motion on [0,1]. The lower bound via cutsets gives the same functional with the minimum over annuli of the field minimum, i.e. a different functional. The two bounds do not match: the upper bound is a maximum of a Brownian motion and the lower bound is a minimum, so the limit distribution is sandwiched between beta sqrt g times max and min of a Brownian motion but not identified. The notes' guess of a CGFF limit for the field x -> log R_eff is consistent with this sandwich only if the resistance is dominated by the coarse scale. Key identity: beta sqrt g min_{[0,1]} B <= liminf (log N)^{-1/2} log R_eff <= beta sqrt g max_{[0,1]} B in distribution (heuristic sandwich). Obstruction: Upper (flow) and lower (cutset) bounds converge to different functionals of the concentric walk.

entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Lower-bound the complexity by the OSSS inequality with the sharp four-arm exponent and compare with the exploration-path algorithm. A better lower bound would follow from the OSSS inequality Var f <= sum_i delta_i I_i if one could bound the revealments delta_i by C(A)/n^2 uniformly, giving C(A) >= n^2 Var f / (sum_i I_i) = n^2 / (n^2 alpha_4(n)) = n^{5/4}, which is WEAKER than 6/4. entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Borel-Cantelli over the Hermitisation: identify which estimate is only in probability. entries.title: Attempt on Ballisticity under the ellipticity moment condition
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Examine whether the moment condition controls the back-and-forth trap time and hence the regeneration-time tail. Result: The quantity 1/(1 - omega(0,e) omega(0,-e)) is the expected number of returns of the two-site back-and-forth excursion between 0 and e, so the moment condition bounds the expected holding time in two-site traps but not in larger traps (a trap of k sites in a line has holding time controlled by products of k such ratios, whose expectation is not bounded by the first-moment condition). Proposition 2.21 of the source shows the condition is necessary; sufficiency would need a bound on the expected time spent in traps of every size, i.e. on E[tau_1 | D = infinity]. A natural sufficient strengthening is a moment condition on the exit time from every finite box, which is implied by the two-site condition only under an additional assumption on the transition probabilities to move away. I therefore see the question as open in the sense that the two-site condition is strictly weaker than what the regeneration argument needs, and the Dirichlet case works because of the specific reversal identity of Dirichlet environments (Sabot's exit-time integrability). No new result. Obstruction: Two-site moment condition does not control larger traps; the Dirichlet argument uses a special reversal identity.

Recorded reduction: (P)_M for large M <=> E[tau_1^{M'}] < infinity for some M' growing with M, so the question is a moment self-improvement question. entries.title: Attempt on A peeling algorithm exploring site percolation on Boltzmann maps
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Design the algorithm and check whether the exploration frontier remains Markov. Result: For bond percolation the peeling frontier is a two-colour boundary (free/blocked edges) and the algorithm peels the edge at the colour change, keeping the unexplored region a Boltzmann map with a boundary of the same type. For site percolation the colour lives on vertices and after peeling a face the newly exposed boundary vertices are uncoloured; the natural algorithm peels the edge whose left endpoint is black and right endpoint is uncoloured, colouring the new vertices as they appear. The unexplored region is then a Boltzmann map with a boundary condition that is a word in {black, white, uncoloured}, and the difficulty is that the length of the black segment is no longer a Markov chain by itself: the future depends on the positions of uncoloured vertices along the boundary. The frontier becomes Markov if one records the boundary word, which is an infinite-dimensional state. On triangulations the problem was solved (Angel-Curien) because degree-3 faces expose at most one new vertex per step, keeping the state finite; for general Boltzmann maps with large faces a peeled face exposes many uncoloured vertices at once. So a Markov site-percolation peeling exists exactly when faces expose boundedly many vertices, i.e. for bounded face degrees, and the general Boltzmann case requires a state space of boundary words; whether the threshold can still be computed from a word-valued Markov chain is the open part. Obstruction: Unbounded face degrees expose many uncoloured boundary vertices at once; the frontier state is a word, not an integer.

Result: The Z^d proof of u* > 0 (Sznitman) uses a renormalisation over boxes at scales L_n with the decoupling of the interlacement in distant boxes controlled by the capacity of boxes (order L^{d-2}) against the volume of the sprinkling; on G x Z the walk has spectral dimension d_s = 2 log 3 / log 5 + 1 = 2.365 and walk dimension d_w = log 5 / log 2 = 2.32 in G, and the capacity of a box of side L in G x Z is of order L^{d_f + 1 - d_w} with d_f = log 3/log 2 = 1.585, i.e. L^{0.26}: capacity grows very slowly. The renormalisation needs the number of boxes at scale L_{n+1} covering a box at scale L_n times the probability that interlacement at level u hits a box (about u cap(box)) to be summable; with capacity L^{0.26} and the gasket's self-similar structure one needs the box at scale L_n to be avoided by the vacant-set-crossing with probability decaying faster than the branching of the renormalisation, which fails because the exponent 0.26 is too small to dominate the combinatorial factor of the gasket's cut sets: a crossing of a gasket triangle can be blocked by hitting one of only three corner regions (the gasket has cut points), so the vacant set is blocked whenever the interlacement hits the three corner neighbourhoods, which at level u happens with probability roughly 1 - exp(-3u cap(corner region)) -> a constant not tending to zero as the scale grows only if cap(corner region) stays bounded; since cap grows like L^{0.26} it tends to infinity and the blocking probability tends to 1. This argues for u* = 0 on G x Z: at any u > 0, at large scales every corner region is hit and the gasket's cut-point structure disconnects the vacant set. The argument is heuristic because the corner regions of the Z-direction are cylinders, not points, and a vacant path can bypass a corner through the Z direction; the honest conclusion is that the answer hinges on whether the Z direction provides bypasses of the gasket's cut points, which I could not settle. Key identity: Capacity of a box of side L in G x Z is about L^{0.26}; the gasket's cut points force vacant crossings through corner regions whose hitting probability tends to 1. Obstruction: The Z-direction bypass of gasket cut points is not quantified; the sign of the answer is unclear.

entries.title: Attempt on Critical exponent beta = 1 in the asymptotic sense for high-dimensional percolation
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Differentiate the magnetisation lace expansion at the critical point. Result: The bounded-ratio statement beta = 1 follows from the triangle condition via the Barsky-Aizenman differential inequality dtheta/dp >= c theta - C theta^2 together with the mean-field upper bound; an asymptotic statement needs the limit of theta(p)/(p - p_c), i.e. a differentiable extension of theta at p_c from the right with a computable derivative. With the magnetisation M(p,h) (ghost field h), the lace expansion for the two-point function gives an expansion of the susceptibility chi(p,h) = dM/dh whose coefficients are analytic in p near p_c for fixed h > 0; theta(p) = M(p,0+) is the h -> 0 limit, and the interchange of the h -> 0 and p -> p_c limits is exactly where asymptotic control is lost: the expansion converges uniformly for h >= h_0 > 0 but the coefficients' h-dependence near h = 0 is only bounded, not differentiable. A candidate route: the scaling relation beta = gamma - Delta with gamma = 1 asymptotically (Hara-Slade) and Delta = 2 asymptotically (gap exponent, known asymptotically in the sense of the ratio only) would give beta = 1 asymptotically if the gap exponent were known asymptotically; I checked that the gap exponent's asymptotic form is equivalent to the asymptotic form of the ratio M_3/M_2^2 ... in the source's notation, which is itself not derived. Reduction: asymptotic beta = 1 <=> asymptotic gap exponent Delta = 2 via the magnetisation differential inequality with sharp constant. Obstruction: The h -> 0 and p -> p_c limits do not commute in the lace expansion; the sharp constant in the gap-exponent inequality is missing.

entries.title: Attempt on Infrared bound for nearest-neighbour percolation in every dimension d > 6
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Examine the small parameter of the lace expansion and whether a different expansion parameter exists for d in {7,...,10}. Result: The lace expansion converges when the triangle diagram at p_c is small, which for nearest-neighbour percolation is controlled by the random-walk quantities: the triangle at p_c is bounded by a constant times (2d)^{-1} times sum over n of the return probabilities, i.e. by beta_d = O(1/d); the NoBLE refinement replaces 1/d by a numerically computed constant and the bootstrap closes for d >= 11 because the computed bound on the triangle at d = 10 exceeds the threshold. Below d = 11 there is no small parameter: the triangle diagram is of order 1 but finite for d > 6, and finiteness alone does not make the expansion converge; convergence needs smallness. An alternative is to bootstrap from d = 11 downward using a continuous interpolation in the dimension (long-range or spread-out interpolation), but the interpolated models at d = 10 are spread-out models, whose infrared bound is already known, and the interpolation does not return to the nearest-neighbour model at d = 10 without passing through a non-small regime. So the obstruction is structural: the method requires a small parameter and there is none for nearest-neighbour d in {7,...,10}. A rigorous partial statement: the infrared bound holds for the nearest-neighbour model in d in {7,...,10} on any lattice whose triangle diagram at p_c is below the NoBLE threshold, which fails for Z^d but holds for some non-Z^d lattices of higher coordination number (e.g. the body-centred or the D_d-type lattices in d = 7, 8 where the coordination number is larger); I did not verify the threshold numerically for those lattices. Obstruction: No small parameter for nearest-neighbour Z^d with 7 <= d <= 10.

entries.title: Attempt on Existence and equality of the supercritical exponents gamma', nu', nu_2' in high dimensions
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Try to control the finite-cluster susceptibility above p_c via the lace expansion with a cluster-size cutoff. Result: Above p_c the finite-cluster two-point function tau^f(x) = P(0 <-> x, |C(0)| < infinity) is not directly lace-expandable because the finite-cluster condition is not local; the standard route is through the h -> 0 limit of the magnetisation, whose derivatives in h at fixed p > p_c give the finite-cluster moments. The scaling relation gamma' = gamma follows if the magnetisation M(p,h) has a scaling form M ~ (p - p_c) f(h / (p - p_c)^Delta) with the same Delta on both sides, which is the mean-field prediction; the mean-field magnetisation satisfies M ~ (p-p_c) + sqrt(h) crossover, and the finite-cluster susceptibility above p_c would then be chi^f ~ (p - p_c)^{-1}, i.e. gamma' = 1. A rigorous one-sided bound is available: chi^f(p) >= c/(p - p_c) from the differential inequality of Aizenman-Barsky applied above p_c (since dtheta/dp is bounded by chi^f up to constants and theta ~ (p - p_c)); the matching upper bound needs the finite-cluster expansion. So gamma' >= 1 in the bounded-ratio sense is rigorous; gamma' <= 1 is the open half. Similarly nu' >= nu follows from the lower bound on the finite-cluster correlation length via the same inequality chain. Key identity: dtheta/dp <= C chi^f(p) and theta ~ (p - p_c) give chi^f(p) >= c/(p - p_c), i.e. gamma' >= 1 in the ratio sense. Obstruction: No expansion for finite-cluster quantities above p_c; only the lower bounds are rigorous.

entries.title: Attempt on Sharp intrinsic and extrinsic one-arm exponents in high dimensions
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Reduce the intrinsic limit to a renewal-type statement for the branching-process comparison. Result: The intrinsic one-arm probability is bounded above and below by constants over n (Kozma-Nachmias), and the comparison object is the survival probability of a critical branching process with finite variance, for which n P(survive n generations) -> 2/sigma^2 (Kolmogorov). For the intrinsic arm event the analogous statement would be n P(intrinsic radius >= n) -> a_in where a_in should be 2/V with V the variance of the offspring distribution of the effective branching structure (the cluster explored by intrinsic distance is a branching process with dependent offspring). Existence of the limit therefore reduces to a Kolmogorov-type limit theorem for the intrinsic exploration, which needs the mean-field two-point asymptotics at the level of an exact constant (the lace expansion gives tau_{p_c}(x) ~ A/|x|^{d-2} with an exact constant A, Hara 2008), plus an exact constant for the 'variance' of the exploration, which is the sum of the three-point function's connected part, computable from the lace expansion in principle. The extrinsic limit is harder because the extrinsic arm event mixes intrinsic distance and Euclidean displacement; its bounded-ratio form comes from a second-moment argument that does not give constants. I could not complete either constant. Obstruction: Exact constants for the intrinsic branching structure require second-order lace expansion information.

entries.title: Attempt on Notions of criticality for percolation on high-dimensional tori
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Compute the maximiser of d/dp log chi_T(p) in the mean-field random-graph analogue and compare with the window width. Result: For the Erdos-Renyi graph G(n, p) the susceptibility chi(p) = E|C(uniform vertex)| satisfies chi ~ 1/(1 - np) below the window and the derivative of log chi is maximised inside the critical window np = 1 + O(n^{-1/3}), at distance O(n^{-1/3}) from any other reasonable critical point; the same holds for the torus IF the torus susceptibility has the mean-field form chi_T(p) = chi_{Z^d}(p) + V (theta-like term) with the crossover at |p - p_c| ~ V^{-1/3}, which is the content of the torus plateau results (Theorem 13.9 of the source and the 2021 Hutchcroft-Michta-Slade torus plateau). Given the plateau, log chi_T is increasing with derivative of order 1/(p_c - p) below the window and of order V^{1/3} inside it, then decreasing above; so the maximiser lies within O(V^{-1/3}) of p_c(Z^d) provided the derivative inside the window is controlled from below, which requires the plateau statement with derivatives, i.e. a two-sided bound on d chi_T/dp inside the window. The plateau results bound chi_T itself, not its derivative; Russo's formula expresses the derivative as an expected number of pivotals, which in the window is of order chi_T times V^{1/3}, but only up to constants and only as an upper bound from the known results. Reduction: Open Problem 13.1 for p_c^{(1)} follows from a two-sided pivotal count inside the window. Obstruction: Two-sided derivative control of the torus susceptibility inside the scaling window is not available.

entries.title: Attempt on Scaling limit of critical percolation cluster sizes on the hypercube
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Compare the exploration process of the hypercube with the Aldous exploration of the Erdos-Renyi graph. Result: Aldous's proof for G(n,p) uses that the exploration process is a random walk with drift theta - t and unit variance, up to depletion; on the hypercube the exploration of a cluster is a random walk whose step distribution depends on the local geometry (the number of unexplored neighbours of the current vertex is d minus the number of explored ones, and explored vertices are geometrically correlated). In the window the explored set has size V^{2/3} = 2^{2d/3}, which is a vanishing fraction of V, but the DEPLETION seen by a single vertex is not uniform: the explored vertices cluster geometrically, so the walk's drift correction is a functional of the geometry, not of the total explored mass as in G(n,p). This is exactly why the hypercube is harder than the Hamming graph (where the geometry is 'mean-field enough' and the scaling limit was obtained by Federico-van der Hofstad-den Hollander-Hulshof for the Hamming cube). A reduction: the scaling limit follows if the exploration's drift satisfies E[step | past] = theta 2^{-d/3} - (explored mass)/V + o(2^{-d/3}) uniformly over the window, i.e. if the local depletion is asymptotically equal to the global depletion; this is a 'non-backtracking randomness' statement about the geometry of critical hypercube clusters (that they are spread out like independent samples), which is the mean-field cluster geometry conjecture and is open. Obstruction: Local versus global depletion in the exploration walk; needs spread-out geometry of critical hypercube clusters.

entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Reduce to the scaling limit of the IIC itself (C0077) plus a homogenisation of the walk on the limit tree. So the problem is subsumed by C0077 plus a resistance-form convergence theorem (Croydon's framework), which needs the convergence of the IIC as a resistance metric space, a stronger statement than the measure-valued convergence in the source. entries.title: Attempt on Borel summability of the 1/d expansion of the percolation threshold
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Bound the coefficients' growth from the lace expansion's structure and compare with the Borel condition. Result: Borel summability (Watson/Nevanlinna) needs the remainder after N terms to be bounded by C K^N N! (2d)^{-N} uniformly in a sector, and the coefficients to grow at most like K^N N!. The known coefficients a_1 = 1, a_2 = 1, a_3 = 7/2 and the computed higher ones (Mertens-Moore numerics) grow rapidly, consistent with factorial growth. The lace expansion gives the coefficient a_i as a sum over lace diagrams with i-th order random-walk contributions; the number of lace diagrams at order N grows like N! (the laces are essentially permutations of intervals), and each contributes O(1) after the 1/(2d) powers are extracted, so the factorial growth of a_N is plausible, and the remainder estimate of the same form would follow from a bound on the contribution of all diagrams of order >= N by K^N N! (2d)^{-N}. The lace expansion's remainder term is controlled in the existing proofs of the expansion only as O((2d)^{-N}) with an N-dependent constant not tracked; tracking it gives, at best, the factorial bound if the number of order-N diagrams is bounded by K^N N!, which I believe is correct for the diagrams counted with their symmetry factors. The uniform-in-sector (complex d) statement needed for Borel summability is meaningless for the lattice; one would need an analytic continuation in a parameter playing the role of 1/(2d), e.g. the spread-out range or a long-range exponent, and then the Nevanlinna condition in that parameter. So the honest reduction: Borel summability requires (i) K^N N! bounds on the lace-expansion remainder, plausible and unproved, and (ii) an analytic interpolation in the expansion parameter, for which no natural candidate is known. This mirrors the situation for the self-avoiding walk connective constant expansion (Graham's Borel-type bounds) mentioned in the source. Obstruction: No analytic interpolation in 1/(2d); remainder constants not tracked.

The triangle correction: the branching process approximation counts each vertex's d(n-1) neighbours; the neighbours along the same coordinate line are mutually adjacent (a clique K_n), so a cluster exploring along a line finds n-1 vertices at once; this is a finite-size correction of relative order 1/n at each step, giving a_2(d) of order 1 in d; the source's Federico et al. result identifies it. The truncation at d/3 comes from the window width: the critical window of the Hamming graph has width V^{-1/3} = n^{-d/3} in p (relative), so terms beyond order n^{-d/3} are inside the window and meaningless as an expansion of a single critical value; this explains the O(n^{-1-d/3}) error and the number of meaningful terms d/3. Beyond this structural explanation and the second-order term, I did not compute a_3(d); it would need the 4-cycle and two-triangle corrections on the Hamming graph, where 4-cycles through a vertex number about d(d-1)(n-1)^2/2 (two coordinates) plus in-line ones. Key identity: Only terms above the critical window width n^{-d/3} are meaningful, which explains the truncation index d/3. Obstruction: Third-order cycle corrections on K_n^d not computed.

entries.title: Attempt on No infinite cluster at criticality on quasi-transitive graphs with p_c < 1
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Split by growth type and identify the remaining cases precisely. Result: By Trofimov's theorem a quasi-transitive graph of polynomial growth is quasi-isometric to a Cayley graph of a virtually nilpotent group, and the critical behaviour of percolation is not a quasi-isometry invariant in general, so this does not reduce directly to Z^d; however the known proof for Z^2 (Harris-Kesten) and the high-dimensional proof (lace expansion, d >= 11) do not transfer either. Exponential growth is Hutchcroft's theorem. The remaining cases are (a) polynomial growth of degree 3 to 10 (and all virtually nilpotent non-abelian cases, e.g. the Heisenberg group of growth degree 4), where the problem is at least as hard as C0023, and (b) intermediate growth (Grigorchuk-type groups), where Hutchcroft's argument fails because it uses that the number of vertices at distance n grows exponentially to compare the cluster with a branching structure. For case (b) I checked the two known routes: the nonamenable route (Burton-Keane fails, so uniqueness monotonicity gives theta(p_c)=0 through the Benjamini-Lyons-Peres-Schramm argument) does not apply since intermediate-growth groups are amenable; the exponential-growth route uses a subadditivity argument on the expected number of vertices at distance n reached by the cluster, which requires growth rate > 1 in the exponential sense. Intermediate growth groups have growth exp(n^alpha), alpha < 1, which is superpolynomial, and Hutchcroft's argument actually needs only that the growth is faster than any polynomial? His proof uses the growth to show that the susceptibility is finite at p_c in a spherically-averaged sense via a comparison with a branching random walk with killing at rate given by the growth; I believe the argument requires exponential growth for the comparison to be uniform, so intermediate growth is a genuine gap. Recorded: the open cases are polynomial growth (degree 3 to 10 and non-abelian nilpotent) and intermediate growth. Obstruction: Polynomial growth is the Z^d problem; intermediate growth defeats the exponential-growth comparison.

entries.title: Attempt on Lace expansion for the random-cluster model with q not in {1,2}
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Identify what makes q = 1 and q = 2 expandable and whether a q-analogue of the random-current switching lemma exists. Result: q = 1 is Bernoulli percolation (independence gives the pivotal decomposition); q = 2 is expandable through the random-current representation and the switching lemma (Sakai's lace expansion for the Ising model). For integer q >= 3 the Potts model has a random-current-like representation (the 'random-current representation for Potts' via the Edwards-Sokal coupling with q colours) but the switching lemma fails because currents are Z_q-valued and the pairing structure that gives the switching identity is specific to Z_2. A lace expansion needs a 'pivotal' notion for which the model factorises across the pivotal: in FK with general q the cluster weight q^{k(omega)} couples the two sides of a pivotal edge only through the count of clusters, which changes by one when the pivotal is closed; this suggests an expansion in which each pivotal carries a factor q or 1 depending on whether closing it splits a cluster, i.e. a lace expansion for the two-point function with the cluster count as an extra variable, which is exactly the generating function in the number of clusters, i.e. the Tutte polynomial. So the expansion would be an expansion of the Tutte polynomial's two-point version, which is #P-hard to evaluate in general, suggesting no simple diagrammatic expansion exists for generic q; for the infrared bound one might instead use reflection positivity (available for integer q and for the FK model on Z^d with q >= 1 via the Potts representation), which gives the infrared bound for the Potts spin-spin covariance directly for integer q >= 1 (Frohlich-Simon-Spencer), without a lace expansion. Recorded: for integer q the infrared bound is available by reflection positivity (this is classical), so the source's 'and use it to derive an infrared bound' is partly moot for integer q; the genuinely open content is the expansion itself and the non-integer q infrared bound. Key identity: Reflection positivity gives the infrared bound for integer-q Potts covariances without any expansion; the open part is non-integer q and the expansion. Obstruction: No switching lemma for Z_q currents; the natural expansion variable is a Tutte-polynomial quantity.

entries.title: Attempt on Convergence of height-fraction statistics in the sandpile scaling limit
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Use the Apollonian structure of the limit to predict the local statistics in each patch. Result: The Pegden-Smart limit is a piecewise-quadratic function whose Hessian takes values in the set Gamma of integer superharmonic matrices; inside a patch where the Hessian is a fixed matrix A in Gamma, the sandpile is (Levine-Pegden-Smart) a periodic pattern determined by A, so the height-j fraction in a patch converges to the frequency of height j in that periodic pattern, which is a computable rational number. Hence the refinement holds in the interior of every patch; the question reduces to the boundary set between patches (the Apollonian gasket of patch boundaries), which has Lebesgue measure zero in the limit but whose discrete neighbourhood might carry a positive fraction of sites at scale n if the boundary layers have width of order n^{alpha}, alpha > 0... the patches are of all sizes (Apollonian), and the total area of patches of diameter < eps tends to zero as eps -> 0 (the gasket has Hausdorff dimension < 2), so for any delta the fraction of sites within the small patches is < delta for eps small, and within large patches the convergence holds; therefore the height-j fraction converges PROVIDED the discrete configuration inside a large patch is exactly the periodic pattern except in a boundary layer of o(n) width, which is the content of the Levine-Pegden-Smart 'Apollonian structure in the abelian sandpile' theorem (they prove the patterns appear; the width of the transition layers is what I could not confirm from memory). Conditional resolution recorded: the height-fraction convergence follows from the patch-pattern theorem plus an o(n) transition-layer bound plus the measure-zero gasket; the identity-element scaling limit remains open beyond the Caracciolo-Paoletti-Sportiello special case. Key identity: Inside a patch with Hessian A the height-j frequency is the frequency of j in the A-pattern; the gasket of boundaries has area zero, so convergence reduces to o(n) transition layers. Obstruction: Transition-layer width between patches not confirmed; identity element limit open.

entries.title: Attempt on Maximal integer superharmonic matrices in dimensions d >= 3
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Test the d = 3 analogue of the Apollonian structure on the simplest candidates (diagonal matrices). Result: Gamma(Z^d) is the set of symmetric matrices A for which there is an integer-valued function on Z^d whose discrete Laplacian is at most the constant ... with quadratic growth A: g(x) = (1/2) x^T A x + (lower order) integer-valued superharmonic. Diagonal A = diag(a_1,...,a_d): g(x) = sum_i (1/2) a_i x_i^2 rounded is integer-valued; the discrete Laplacian of x -> ceil(a x^2 / 2) in one dimension is at most a + 1 ... in one dimension the maximal a with an integer superharmonic quadratic of curvature a is determined by the 1D odometer; for diagonal matrices the problem separates into d one-dimensional problems and the maximal diagonal elements are rational (the 1D maximal curvatures are rational, e.g. the 1D sandpile has only finitely many patterns). This gives rational maximal elements on the diagonal slice, but maximality in Gamma(Z^d) (not just among diagonal matrices) is not implied: a diagonal A might be dominated by a non-diagonal B. In d = 2 the LPS classification shows the maximal elements are dense in the boundary and rational; for d = 3 the analogue of the Apollonian packing would be a packing by spheres of a slab, whose tangency structure has more degrees of freedom (a sphere touching four others is not determined by rational data in general: Descartes-type relations in 3D involve a quadratic form on curvatures with generic irrational solutions unless the initial spheres are chosen integrally). This suggests that rationality may FAIL in d = 3 unless the initial configuration forces integrality via the Soddy-Gosset relation with integer curvatures; the analogue of the band packing in d = 3 has initial curvatures determined by the lattice (integer), and integral Apollonian-type packings in 3D do have all curvatures integral when the initial ones are (Soddy-Gosset gives a quadratic recursion preserving integrality). So rationality is plausible in d = 3 if the correspondence to packings persists, and isolation would be false (packings are dense in the boundary). Recorded as a conjectural picture with the Soddy-Gosset integrality argument as the reason to expect rational entries. Key identity: If the d = 3 maximal elements correspond to a sphere packing generated from integer initial curvatures, Soddy-Gosset integrality gives rational entries. Obstruction: No d = 3 analogue of the LPS correspondence between Gamma(Z^d) and packings.

entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Analyse the covariance of the dyadic prime-block increments and the failure of independence. Result: Decoupling Q by splitting the index set into two halves I, J gives P(Q = z) <= P(|sum_{i in I, j in J} c_ij xi_i xi'_j - ...| small)^{1/2}-type bounds where, conditionally on the J-variables, the bilinear form is a linear form in the I-variables with coefficients a_i = sum_j c_ij xi_j; the linear Littlewood-Offord (Erdos) bound gives P <= C/sqrt(number of nonzero a_i), and the a_i are nonzero with high probability except on an event where many coefficient sums vanish, whose probability is itself controlled by a Littlewood-Offord bound on the rows; the loss comes from the union over rows and the conditioning, which is where the n^{o(1)} or logarithmic factors enter in the known proofs. The extremal example (xi_1 + ... + xi_n)^2 shows n^{-1/2} is the right order because the square of a sum concentrates on O(sqrt n) values. To remove the logarithm one needs a rank-type inverse theorem: if P(Q = z) >= n^{-1/2} C then the coefficient matrix is close to rank one with arithmetic structure, and the inverse theorems available (Nguyen-Vu) give such structure only at the cost of a logarithmic loss in the threshold. No improvement obtained; the reduction to a lossless inverse theorem is recorded. Obstruction: The known inverse Littlewood-Offord theorems carry logarithmic losses.

entries.title: Attempt on Rate of convergence in the circular law as a function of the moment assumption
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Locate the rate bottleneck in the Hermitisation argument. Result: The Hermitisation proof controls the log-potential U_n(z) = (1/n) log|det(n^{-1/2}M_n - z)| through the singular-value distribution of the shifted matrix; the error has three parts: (a) the rate in the Marchenko-Pastur-type convergence of the singular-value distribution, of order n^{-1/2}-ish under four moments and degrading to n^{-c(eps)} under 2+eps moments through the truncation at level n^{1/(2+eps)}; (b) the smallest singular value lower bound, which contributes only a log-factor to the log-potential error; (c) the conversion from log-potential convergence to weak convergence of the ESD, which costs a power through the smoothing of the Laplacian. The truncation in (a) is the eps-dependent bottleneck: entries are truncated at n^{1/(2+eps)}, the truncated variance differs from 1 by O(n^{-eps/(2+eps)}), and this variance error propagates to the singular-value distribution as a shift of the same order, giving delta of order eps/(2+eps) times the conversion loss in (c). So one expects delta(eps) = c eps/(2+eps) for small eps with c < 1 from step (c), and a plateau at the four-moment rate for eps >= 2. This is a heuristic scaling, not a theorem; the exact constant c requires the sharpest version of (c), which is the Kolmogorov-distance version of the log-potential-to-measure conversion. Key identity: Truncation at n^{1/(2+eps)} induces a variance error n^{-eps/(2+eps)}, which caps delta(eps) at a constant times eps/(2+eps) for small eps. Obstruction: Sharp conversion constant from log-potential to Kolmogorov distance.

entries.title: Attempt on Deterministic (1+epsilon)-approximation of the cover time
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Examine whether the Gaussian free field characterisation can be made asymptotically exact. Result: DLP show t_cov ≍ |E| (E max GFF)^2; the later result of Ding (2012, 'Asymptotics of cover times via Gaussian free fields: bounded-degree graphs and general trees') gives asymptotic equality t_cov ~ |E| (E max eta)^2 for bounded-degree graphs when t_cov/t_hit -> infinity, and Zhai (2018) proved the asymptotic formula for general graphs under the same condition. Given the asymptotic formula, a (1+eps) approximation of t_cov reduces to a (1+eps) approximation of E max of a Gaussian vector with given covariance (the Green function), which is a deterministic computational problem: computing E max of a Gaussian vector to within 1+eps is not known to be in deterministic polynomial time in general (the majorizing-measure/generic-chaining bounds are only within constants; exact computation of Gaussian maxima expectations is #P-hard in some formulations). So the question reduces, for graphs with t_cov/t_hit -> infinity, to the deterministic approximability of E max of a Gaussian vector with a graph-Laplacian covariance; a positive answer would follow from a deterministic FPTAS for Gaussian expected maxima on such covariances, which is open; graphs with t_cov ≍ t_hit (e.g. cycles, where the cover time is dominated by hitting times) need a separate treatment and are the easier case since hitting times are computable exactly. Reduction recorded. Key identity: t_cov ~ |E| (E max GFF)^2 when t_cov/t_hit -> infinity (Ding; Zhai), so (1+eps)-approximation reduces to approximating a Gaussian expected maximum. Obstruction: No deterministic (1+eps) algorithm for Gaussian expected maxima with general covariance.

entries.title: Attempt on Concentration of the cover time at the scale of the maximal hitting time
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Test the claim on the extreme families and derive the one-sided bound from Matthews-type arguments. Result: Upper tail: for any graph, P(tau_cov > t_cov + s t_hit) <= e^{-cs}? The standard argument: after time 2 t_hit... using the Markov property at multiples of the 'maximal hitting time' scale, the probability that a fixed uncovered vertex remains uncovered for another 2 t_hit is at most 1/2 by Markov's inequality on hitting times, but the union over uncovered vertices costs the number of uncovered vertices, so the naive bound gives only P(tau_cov > t_cov + s t_hit) <= n 2^{-s}, i.e. exponential decay after a log n shift, not at scale t_hit from the mean unless t_cov - t_cov... For the complete graph, tau_cov is a coupon-collector time with standard deviation of order n ~ t_hit, and the centred cover time divided by t_hit converges to a Gumbel, which has exponential tails: consistent. For the cycle Z_n, t_hit ≍ n^2 ≍ t_cov and tau_cov/n^2 converges to a non-degenerate law with exponential tail (the cover time of the cycle is the time for the range to reach n, a functional of Brownian motion with Gaussian-type tails): consistent, and the standard deviation is of order n^2 = t_hit: consistent. For the two-dimensional torus, t_hit ≍ n^2 log n... t_cov ≍ n^2 (log n)^2, and the cover time fluctuations are known to be of order n^2 log n (Belius-Kistler / Abe: the cover time of the 2D torus has fluctuations of order t_hit... the second-order term is of order n^2 log n times a random variable), consistent with the question. So the conjecture passes all the standard test cases; the general lower-tail statement (tau_cov not much smaller than t_cov) is the hard side because early coverage requires all vertices to be hit quickly, which involves correlations of hitting times; via the GFF isomorphism (Ding-Lee-Peres) the cover time corresponds to the level at which the GFF maximum exceeds a threshold, and concentration of the cover time at scale t_hit corresponds to tightness of the GFF maximum at scale sqrt(t_hit/|E|), which is tightness of the maximum of the Gaussian free field on the graph in the correct units; tightness of the GFF maximum is known for the 2D torus and trees but not for general graphs. Reduction: the question is essentially equivalent to tightness of the graph GFF maximum in units of the maximal hitting time. Key identity: Via the second Ray-Knight isomorphism, concentration of tau_cov at scale t_hit corresponds to tightness of the GFF maximum on the graph at the corresponding scale. Obstruction: Tightness of the GFF maximum on general graphs is not known.

entries.title: Attempt on Chaos in directed polymers in dimensions d >= 3
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Check which steps of the d = 2 proof are dimension-dependent. Result: The source's d = 1+1 proof establishes superconcentration of the free energy (variance o(n)) via hypercontractivity and then chaos from superconcentration through the general equivalence theorem; the dimension-dependent step is the variance bound Var(log Z_n) = O(n/log n), obtained from the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm influence inequality applied to the free energy with the influence of a single site bounded by the expected overlap of two polymers at that site, whose sum over sites is the expected overlap, of order n in the strong disorder regime. The BKS argument is dimension-free provided the polymer is in the strong disorder phase (positive overlap); in d >= 3 the strong disorder phase exists at low temperature (Comets-Yoshida), so the variance bound O(n/log n) transfers and superconcentration follows; the equivalence theorem then gives chaos at the level of the overlap between the polymers at slightly perturbed environments. So the obstruction the source mentions ('certain parts do not work in higher dimensions') must be in the identification that the overlap in the strong-disorder phase is of order n (needed for the influence sum to be order n and the BKS gain to be meaningful): in d >= 3 at low temperature the overlap is positive but the known lower bounds are only qualitative (positive limit of the overlap along the endpoint), not quantitative along the whole path. Rigorous partial: superconcentration (Var log Z_n = o(n)) in d >= 3 at low temperature follows from BKS if the expected path overlap is of order n, which is a consequence of the strong disorder characterisation via the endpoint overlap only if the overlap is positive at a positive fraction of times; this last step is plausible but I found no reference proving it in d >= 3. Reduction recorded. Obstruction: Quantitative (order n) path overlap in the strong disorder phase for d >= 3.

entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Attempt the second-moment bound on the overlap via Gaussian interpolation. entries.title: Attempt on Bridges between multiple peaks in the NK fitness landscape
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Estimate the number of near-maximal configurations and compare with the connectivity threshold of the level set on the hypercube. Result: In the NK model with K = O(1) the fitness is a sum of n local terms each depending on K + 1 bits, so the field is a sum of n independent contributions (for the standard model with random neighbourhoods) and the level set at height M_n - delta_n with delta_n = o(n) but delta_n >> sqrt n contains exp(c delta_n^2/n)... the number of configurations within delta of the maximum is, by a large-deviation count, about exp(n I(delta/n)) for a rate I; bridges exist if this level set percolates on the hypercube, and a level set of density rho on the n-cube contains a giant connected component when the local structure allows, roughly when each configuration in the set has on average more than one neighbour in the set: the expected number of neighbours in the level set of a typical level-set point is n times the conditional probability that flipping one bit stays within delta of the maximum, which is n times (probability that the change of the K+1 affected local terms is at most delta), of order n delta/n = delta when delta is small compared to the local term scale... so bridges exist (heuristically) when delta_n >> 1, i.e. the level set within a constant deficit of the maximum is connected in the giant-component sense for deficits growing to infinity, while for bounded deficits the peaks are isolated. entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Check whether the ergodic-environment argument for the two-sided statement (Theorem 2.3/3.2) localises to one side. entries.title: Attempt on Recurrence-transience criterion for excited random walks under stationary ergodic environments
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Examine the branching-process-with-migration proof and where i.i.d. is used. Result: The proof of Theorem 3.10 under (3.10) translates the walk into a branching process with migration whose offspring law at site k is determined by the cookie stack at k; under (IID) the branching process is homogeneous in space and the criterion delta > 1 is the criterion for the branching process to die out... under (SE) the process is a branching process in a stationary ergodic environment (BPRE with migration), whose survival criterion is governed by the Lyapunov exponent of the environment, i.e. by an ergodic average of log-means, not by the mean delta of the drift. So the natural (SE) analogue is NOT 'delta in [-1,1]' with delta = E sum_i (2 omega(0,i) - 1) but a criterion involving the annealed versus quenched growth rate of the associated BPRE; for i.i.d. environments the two coincide because the migration term is affine. I tested this on the simplest non-i.i.d. case: an environment alternating deterministically between two cookie stacks a and b (period 2, hence SE after a random shift): the branching process with migration is then periodic and its two-step transition is again a branching process with migration with delta_2 = delta_a + delta_b; the criterion becomes delta_a + delta_b > 2 for transience, i.e. the average delta > 1, consistent with the naive extension. For genuinely random ergodic environments a similar averaging holds if the migration is additive, which it is (the number of cookies eaten per visit adds). So the expected answer is YES for (SE) with the same delta, and the obstruction to a proof is that the branching-process comparison uses independence between the offspring at different sites when computing the extinction probability of the process with migration; with dependence one needs an ergodic theorem for the total progeny, available via the Kesten-Kozlov-Spitzer approach only for i.i.d.. Recorded: periodic environments satisfy the naive extension; the general (SE) case reduces to an ergodic total-progeny theorem for branching with migration in stationary environments. Key identity: Periodic two-stack environment: transient iff delta_a + delta_b > 2, i.e. the averaged delta criterion holds. Obstruction: Ergodic total-progeny theorem for branching processes with migration in stationary environments.

entries.title: Attempt on Escape probability of a transient one-dimensional excited random walk
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Express the escape probability through the branching-process representation for the one-cookie deterministic case. Result: In the deterministic environment with one cookie of strength p at each site (M = 1, delta = 2p - 1... transient iff delta > 1 which needs more than one cookie; take M = 2 cookies of strength p each, delta = 2(2p - 1) > 1 iff p > 3/4). The event of never returning to 0 after the first step: the walk must never come back, which in the branching-process picture (right excursions counted by the number of down-crossings of each edge) means the branching process with migration started from the edge (0,1) never produces a down-crossing of (0,1) into 0... the escape probability equals the probability that the total number of down-crossings of the edge (0,1) is zero, which is P(the branching process with migration started at 1 individual at level 1 has zero descendants at level 0) - not directly a standard extinction probability but a hitting probability of the time-reversed process. For the source's example [Zer05, Th. 18] the closed form exists; for general bounded stacks the escape probability is the solution of a finite-dimensional fixed-point equation obtained by conditioning on the first cookie stack at sites 1, 2, ...: define q_k = P(never return to 0 | walk currently at k, all cookies at sites >= k intact, cookies at sites < k in their post-visit states); the states of the sites already visited matter only through the remaining cookie counts, which for M bounded is a finite vector, and the walk's returns to 0 require descending through all visited sites; the escape probability then equals the probability of survival of a Markov chain on finite cookie-count vectors, computable numerically for given (M, p) but with no closed form in general. Recorded: reduction to a finite-state escape problem; closed form only in special cases. Obstruction: No closed form beyond special cases; the reduction gives a numerical procedure only.

entries.title: Attempt on Recurrence-transience dichotomy for excited random walks in dimension d >= 2
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Compare with the RWRE 0-1 law in d >= 3 (C0044) and locate the extra difficulty from self-interaction. Result: For Markovian RWRE the dichotomy question is the directional 0-1 law (C0044, open in d >= 3). For excited random walks the process is not Markov, and even the statement 'either recurrent or transient' (return to the origin infinitely often a.s. or finitely often a.s.) is not implied by any Markov-chain dichotomy; the source's Definition 3.1 asks for a 0-1 law for the number of returns. A route: the event {X returns to 0 infinitely often} is determined by the walk in the environment, and by the ergodicity of the environment its probability does not depend on the starting point in the sense P_x(return to x i.o.) is constant in x; but P_0(return to 0 i.o.) in (0,1) is not excluded by that. The Kalikow-type argument for RWRE (P_0(A_l union A_{-l}) in {0,1}) uses that the walk from 0 and from a far point in the same environment can be coupled after a hitting event; for excited walks the coupled walks see different cookie states (one walk has eaten cookies), which is the extra difficulty. Under (UEL) and boundedness of the stacks (M cookies per site), a walk that has visited a region changes the environment there in a bounded way, and once the walk leaves a region for good the modified cookies are irrelevant; so for transient behaviour the modification is harmless, while recurrence requires infinitely many returns through modified regions. I could not produce a proof; the sharpest statement I can defend: if the excited walk is transient in the sense |X_n| -> infinity with positive probability, then, under (IID) and (UEL), it is transient a.s., by the following argument: on the event of transience the walk eventually leaves every ball, and the environment outside any ball is untouched and i.i.d., so the probability of transience given the walk is at distance R from the origin at a time after which it never returns to the ball... this does not close either because the walk's future depends on the eaten cookies inside the ball only if it returns. Recorded as attempted without result. Obstruction: Self-interaction breaks the coupling arguments behind Markovian 0-1 laws.

entries.title: Attempt on Transience and recurrence of the M(d1,d2) balanced excited random walks
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Analyse M(1,1) on Z^2 through the range of the first-coordinate walk. Result: In M(1,1) the first coordinate moves only at first visits and the second at later visits; the set of visited vertices is the range, and the first-coordinate process is a simple random walk on Z run at the rate of new visits. Recurrence of M(1,1) would follow if the walk returns to the origin infinitely often; since the second coordinate performs a simple random walk on the column above the current first coordinate whenever the vertex was visited before, the walk behaves in each column like a 1D random walk (recurrent) until it hits an unvisited vertex, at which time the first coordinate steps. The number of new visits up to time n is the range R_n; the first coordinate after n steps is a simple random walk at time R_n, so |X^1_n| is of order sqrt(R_n), and the range of a planar walk-like process is at most n, giving |X^1_n| <= sqrt n; a return to the origin requires both coordinates to vanish. A heuristic: if R_n ≍ n/log n as for planar simple random walk then the first coordinate is diffusive at the slower clock, and the walk is 'more recurrent' than planar simple random walk, supporting the conjecture; but the range of M(1,1) is not that of simple random walk because the exploration is column-wise. A rigorous partial fact: M(1,1) is recurrent if and only if the first coordinate returns to 0 infinitely often at times when the second coordinate is 0; since within a column the second coordinate is a recurrent 1D walk that keeps returning to 0 until it finds a new vertex, and new vertices in a column are found at the ends of the visited interval, the question is whether the first-coordinate walk (which is a simple random walk in the clock of new visits) visits 0 infinitely often, which it does a.s. (1D recurrence), and whether at those visits the second coordinate is 0 - not automatic. So recurrence of M(1,1) reduces to: at the (infinitely many) times the first coordinate is 0, the second coordinate, which then performs a 1D walk in the column of 0 with the visited interval of that column, returns to height 0 before finding a new vertex - which has probability bounded below by a constant each time if the visited interval around height 0 in column 0 has length bounded... the visited interval in column 0 grows, and the probability of returning to 0 from the boundary of an interval of length L before exiting is of order 1/L... summing over the visits to column 0 gives a divergent series only if the interval lengths grow slowly enough. This is the crux and I did not settle it; the reduction is recorded. Key identity: M(1,1) recurrent iff, at the infinitely many returns of the first coordinate to 0, the second coordinate returns to 0 in column 0 before finding a new vertex; the return probability is of order 1/(visited interval length). Obstruction: Growth rate of the visited interval in column 0 not controlled.

entries.title: Attempt on Ballisticity criterion under the positivity assumption instead of bounded stacks
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Check the branching-process-with-migration proof for its dependence on bounded stacks. Result: Under (BD) the branching process with migration has bounded migration per generation, and the criterion delta > 2 comes from the tail of the total progeny of a critical branching process with migration delta: P(total progeny > n) ≍ n^{-delta/2}... the speed is positive iff the expected total progeny (expected excursion time) is finite iff delta > 2. With unbounded stacks under (POS1) the migration is unbounded but positive; the total progeny tail is then governed by the same exponent if the migration has finite mean, and the natural conjecture is that the criterion persists as long as the expected total drift delta = E sum_i (2 omega(0,i) - 1) is finite, with additional conditions on the tail of the stack size (as in the source's assumption (6.2) with the exponential-moment-type condition on the number of cookies far from 1/2). entries.title: Attempt on Running-maximum limit theorem at the critical parameter delta = 1 under weaker assumptions
entries.statement: ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Identify what the log n scaling comes from and whether it survives without (POS1). Result: The log n factor at delta = 1 comes from the total progeny of the critical branching process with migration delta = 1 having a tail n^{-1/2} with a logarithmic correction, so that the time to make n right excursions is of order n^2 log n, equivalently the maximum after time t is of order sqrt(t)/log t... the source's scaling sqrt n log n for X_{[nt]} reflects the backtracking being negligible at that scale. Under (6.2) the migration has finite mean and the critical tail should persist (same mechanism as C0134). Removing (POS1) allows left-pushing cookies; the walk then has non-negligible backtracking below its maximum, and the limit of X itself (not only its maximum) may differ from the running maximum; the maximum process S should still converge to the running maximum of Brownian motion since the backtracking affects only the difference S - X, whose scale is the length of a typical left excursion, of order sqrt(n) (diffusive) which is o(sqrt n log n). So the expected answer is: the theorem persists under (6.2), and without (POS1) the maximum still converges but X - S is O(sqrt n), negligible at the sqrt n log n scale, so the conclusion for X persists too. The proof would need the branching-process comparison for two-sided cookies (the branching process with migration then has both immigration and emigration), which is the source's [KM11]-type framework; not carried out. Key identity: Backtracking scale sqrt(n) is negligible against the sqrt(n) log n scale of the maximum at delta = 1. Obstruction: Two-sided branching-with-migration comparison not verified under (6.2) without (POS1).
